title: Born at Gujranwala, 1780
hook: smallpox left the boy with one eye, and tradition says he laughed about it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misls closed: bands of equals, and a kingdom starting to show through. Your line was equals, then a kingdom. Whose quiet voice got a real say? Today a new part of the long story begins: Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Day nine hundred seven.

A small boy lies in a fevered room in Gujranwala, a town in the Punjab plains. The sickness is smallpox. He lives, but the histories say it leaves its marks: a scarred face, and the sight gone from one eye. Plenty of children would carry that like a weight. Tradition remembers this one differently. The boy grows up, becomes a ruler, and when people stare at the face, he laughs. The scars stay. The laughter stays too. Today: born at Gujranwala.
screen: `A FEVER IN GUJRANWALA.` → `ONE EYE GONE.` → `TRADITION SAYS HE LAUGHED.`

segments.voice: Start with the place. Gujranwala was the home ground of the Sukerchakia misl, the band led by the boy's father, Maha Singh. So this child was born into the misl world this path has just walked through: riders, rivals, bands of equals meeting at Amritsar. Nobody in that room could have known that the boy would one day pull those bands together under one rule. Then the sickness. The sources agree on the marks it left, and they don't pretend he was handsome. Some accounts describe him as short and plain, with a pitted face. What they remember is how he carried it. Now the story people love to tell. Tradition says someone once asked the Maharaja why God had given him only one eye. And his answer, as the story goes, was that with one eye he sees everyone the same way: Hindu, Muslim and Sikh, all with a single look. It may be a story polished by years of retelling. Keep it as tradition. But notice what it does. It takes a loss and turns it into a joke, and the joke into a promise about how he'll rule. And that promise has roots in the Guru Granth Sahib. In Sohila, the prayer Sikhs say at bedtime, Guru Nanak says that one light is within everyone, and that the light in all is the light of the One. One light in every face. The boy with one eye was raised on that. Whether or not he ever said the line about the eye, it's a very Sikh joke: the eye is less, and the seeing is more.
screen: `THE SUKERCHAKIA HOME GROUND.` · `SMALLPOX, AND A SCARRED FACE.` · `ONE EYE TO SEE ALL ALIKE.` · `ONE LIGHT IN EVERY FACE.` · then, large: `ONE EYE, CLEAR VISION.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a flaw. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing about yourself you'd rather people didn't notice: a scar, a habit, a laugh that's too loud, a thing you're slow at. Don't fix it. Look at it the way a kind friend would. Is there anything funny in it? Anything it's taught you? See if you can let one small smile come, not at yourself, but with yourself. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Gujranwala, the Sukerchakia home ground where Ranjit Singh was born and where smallpox took one eye. Tradition says he laughed about it. Today's word.
Your line: one eye, clear vision. Today, when you catch yourself hiding a flaw, try laughing about it once, gently, out loud. Day nine hundred seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh in histories, songs and stories, and the tale of his one eye is retold as a sign that he looked on people of every faith alike.

fork.setup: you're the young ruler with a scarred face and one eye. someone asks why God gave you only one eye. what do you say?
options: say nothing, and have them sent away.
laugh, and say one eye sees everyone alike.
say it was bad luck, and change the subject.
fork.reveal: tradition says he laughed and said that with one eye he sees Hindu, Muslim and Sikh the same way. the loss became a joke, and the joke a promise.

Claims rule: the year 1780 appears only in the fixed index title; the voice gives no date or age.
Smallpox, the loss of one eye and the scarred face: widely reported in the histories; framed as 'the histories say'. Confirm.
'Some accounts describe him as short and plain, with a pitted face': common in European visitors' descriptions; confirm the framing is respectful.
The one-eye saying (God gave him one eye so he sees Hindu, Muslim and Sikh alike) is popular tradition and clearly marked as such; confirm the wording of the common telling.
Sohila paraphrase (Ang 13): 'sabh mahi jot jot hai soi', one light within all. Confirm Ang and paraphrase.
Index hook kept verbatim in the hook field.
Audit: Sohila is the bedtime (night) prayer, not the evening prayer (that is Rehras); voice corrected.
